summary: Next Season helps farmers in the Argentine Pampas decide today what their soil will look like in 10 years. The farmer draws their field on a satellite map and enters their crops and management. Next Season combines NASA POWER climate data (2001–2025), MODIS NDVI, SRTM/NASADEM elevation and SoilGrids soil data to diagnose drought, frost and heat risk. It then simulates hundreds of three-season crop rotations and recommends the three that best balance water use, soil health, profit and risk, always compared with “keep doing the same”. An illustrated soil profile shows how organic matter, porosity and infiltration would change over 10 years. Clear economic results show that better rotations may cost more at first but pay off over time. The tool complements, and does not replace, the farmer’s and agronomist’s knowledge.
details:
Next Season — “Decide today what your soil will look like in 10 years”

What it does: Next Season is a web tool that helps farmers in the Argentine Pampas (Buenos Aires, Córdoba, Santa Fe, Entre Ríos and La Pampa) choose crop rotations that protect their soil and their income. The farmer draws their field on a satellite map and enters what they grow and how they manage the land. The tool then shows:

  • the field’s climate from 2001 to 2025;
  • three alternative three-season rotations, compared side by side with “keep doing the same”;
  • how the soil would change over the next 10 years under each option.

How it works: Climate comes from NASA POWER: precipitation, temperature, humidity, wind, radiation and soil moisture (GWETTOP/GWETROOT). From it we compute FAO-56 Penman-Monteith evapotranspiration, the water balance, dry-year risk, frost and heat-stress risk, and ENSO effects (NOAA ONI). Soil properties come from SoilGrids, slope from SRTM/NASADEM, and winter ground cover from MODIS NDVI. The engine simulates every possible three-season combination of nine cropping plans (hundreds of options for each field). It scores each one on water use, soil health (months covered, crop residue, diversity), gross margin and dry-year risk. A carbon model (Hénin-Dupuis) projects organic matter, porosity and water infiltration 10 years ahead. A second tool, the Replanting Index (IDR), uses MODIS NDVI to help decide whether a poorly emerged crop is worth replanting.

Benefits and impact: The farmer sees, in plain language and concrete numbers, that a better rotation may cost more in year one but pays back over time: less fertilizer from legumes, more organic matter, better infiltration, fewer months of bare soil and smaller losses in dry years. The goal is to reduce soybean monoculture and soil degradation, and to support decisions between farmers and their agronomists.

Creativity: The story is “the field your children will inherit”. An illustrated soil profile changes year by year from today to year 10, comparing “keep doing the same” with the proposed alternative.

Factors we considered:

  • Local farm practices: no-till, water table depth, renting versus owning the land, crop insurance, herbicide-resistant weeds and livestock.
  • Satellite versus field data: every satellite value can be edited by the farmer.
  • Uncertainty: a confidence traffic light on each result.
  • A clear notice that the tool complements, and does not replace, local knowledge and the agronomist.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript (a single self-contained file, hosted on GitHub Pages) and the Leaflet map library, with an optional Python/FastAPI server version. Data: NASA POWER, MODIS, SRTM/NASADEM, SoilGrids, NOAA ONI and IGN. Generative AI was used as a coding assistant and to create the logo and illustrations, all marked “AI-generated”. Every recommendation comes from transparent agronomic rules, not from AI.
